name: Report Cards and Parent Emails
title: Report Cards and Parent Emails
answer: AI can help teachers draft report card comments, difficult parent emails, recommendation letters, PLC agendas and seating charts, but the teacher supplies the specific detail and revises every draft so it sounds like them. The aim is to save time on structure and wording, not to hand over judgement about a student. Because a comment that could describe any student tells families nothing, the teacher's own knowledge of the student is what makes the result worth sending.

sections.body: Report card comments take hours each grading period, and that time is one of the recurring costs of teaching. AI can take a teacher's notes about a student's progress and turn them into a draft comment quickly, which shortens the first pass. The problem it solves is volume rather than writing quality, since the same task returns every grading period for every student. It also helps with harder writing jobs, such as a calm, clear and respectful reply to a tense parent email. The teacher still decides what the comment says and how it sounds.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day use, a teacher gathers notes on each student's progress, asks an AI tool to shape them into a draft comment, then rewrites it in their own voice. The same approach covers a difficult parent email, where the draft gives a calm starting point that the teacher checks for accuracy and tone. Recommendation letters, PLC agendas and seating charts can be drafted the same way, and the few minutes saved on each add up across a year. The text does not set this out by grade band, so it describes a general routine rather than separate versions for elementary, middle and high school. What changes with age is the content of the notes, not the steps.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or formal evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its claims are about time saved and about the quality of what families receive, not about measured outcomes. The one supporting reference is internal, a pointer to Chapter 16 for how to write recommendation letters that reflect the real student. The observation that generic comments do little for families is presented as a judgement about communication, not as a finding from a trial. The time savings should therefore be read as a reasonable expectation rather than a documented result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Names and sensitive details should stay out of any tool that is not covered by a signed agreement. The teacher revises every comment so it sounds like them and reflects the real student, and the teacher supplies the substance that makes a comment meaningful, such as a book a student loved or a skill they finally mastered. Drafts of parent emails must be reviewed carefully to make sure they are accurate and sound like the teacher. For serious matters, a conversation by phone or in person is usually better than any email. These decisions stay with the teacher, not the tool.
